title: How to Choose a Spaced Repetition App That You'll Use
author: Eva Keiffenheim
summary: Eva Keiffenheim evaluates spaced repetition tools against three criteria that determine long-term learning: the underlying scheduling algorithm (FSRS is optimal), card quality (which AI tools often fail at by generating verbose, multi-concept cards), and personal consistency (the tool must lower friction enough to sustain habit). Memorization is foundational to critical thinking because you cannot reason about what you do not know. Spaced repetition—reviewing material at increasing intervals—moves knowledge from short-term to long-term memory; three years of practice shows dramatic effects on what one can recall in conversation and writing. AI-generated flashcards frequently violate atomic card principles by packing multiple facts into single questions, creating evaluation traps that lead to under- or over-reviewing. Manual control with thoughtful card design remains superior to full automation.
points: Memorization is not rote repetition but the foundation of critical thinking—you cannot evaluate arguments or make connections without relevant facts in long-term memory.
Spaced repetition (reviewing at increasing intervals) is the evidence-based mechanism for moving knowledge from short-term to long-term memory, with dramatic cumulative effects over years.
The FSRS (Free Spaced Repetition Scheduler) algorithm is the research-backed standard; 'proprietary' algorithms with no published research should raise red flags.
AI-generated flashcards typically violate atomic card principles by combining multiple facts into single questions, making it impossible to objectively grade recall and leading to inefficient review.
The best spaced repetition tools offer full manual control with minimal automation, because human judgment in card design is more important than algorithmic optimization.
quotes: I closed the book. Stared at the ceiling. The next day I Googled 'what's the best way to move things from short-term to long-term memory?
You can choose what you remember and store in your long-term memory.
The more you already know, the easier it is to remember new information, because you can attach it to what's already wired in your brain.

A spaced repetition algorithm determines when you see each card again. Too soon, and you waste time reviewing things you already know. Too late, and you've forgotten, so the card resets to square one.

The best tools either give you full control over card creation or offer AI assistance that you can edit and refine—not AI that replaces your judgment entirely.” Archived from Eva Keiffenheim on April 21, 2026 by Tim.
